title: The Measure of the Cosmos: Berlin to Chimborazo and Back
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Berlin and the Rhine: The Making of a Naturalist (1769–1797)

stops.name: Berlin, Schloss Tegel, birth of "the little apothecary"
stops.campa: In the family seat at Tegel, east of Berlin, a second son is born to the Prussian officer Alexander Georg von Humboldt and Marie-Elisabeth von Holwede on the fourteenth of September. He and his elder brother Wilhelm are raised among tutors, herbaria and the flat Brandenburg woods; the boy collects plants and insects so relentlessly that the household nicknames him der kleine Apotheker, the little apothecary. Berlin gives him rigor; Tegel gives him the taste for the wild that will carry him, one day, to two hemispheres and every latitude between them.
suggested_refs: Schloss Tegel, the Humboldt family seat
Alexander Georg von Humboldt family portrait

stops.name: Mainz, setting out with Georg Forster
stops.campa: At twenty, already restless in the university towns of Frankfurt and Göttingen, Humboldt attaches himself to Georg Forster, the naturalist who sailed round the world with Cook, and sets out with him from Mainz down the Rhine and on through Brabant, Holland, England and revolutionary Paris. It is his first true expedition, four months of rivers, ports and a continent in ferment, and Forster's example, the scientist as traveler and the traveler as writer, becomes the pattern of the life not yet chosen. He dedicates his first paper, on the basalts of the Rhine, to his companion.
suggested_refs: Georg Forster, Ansichten vom Niederrhein (1791)
Humboldt, Mineralogische Beobachtungen über einige Basalte am Rhein (1790)

stops.name: Freiberg, the Bergakademie, the mines of Saxony
stops.campa: At the Freiberg School of Mines Humboldt drives himself without mercy: mornings underground among the Saxon galleries, five or six hours of lecture in the afternoon, the surrounding country combed for plants by candle-light and moonlight after that. He masters mineralogy and geology under Werner in barely a year, leaves in 1792 without troubling to take a degree, and is at once appointed a Prussian inspector of mines, a post he uses, over the following years, to invent a safety lamp and a rescue apparatus for miners, and to keep training the eye that will one day read the strata of two continents.
suggested_refs: Bergakademie Freiberg, founded 1765
Humboldt's miner's safety lamp design

stops.name: Berlin, the death of the mother, the fortune, the resignation
stops.campa: Marie-Elisabeth von Humboldt dies on the nineteenth of November; neither son attends the funeral, for the coldness between mother and sons has never thawed, and one of Alexander's correspondents writes bluntly that her death must be welcome to him. It is, in the plainest sense: brother and sister divide a considerable fortune, and Alexander is at last free of the civil service and of every obligation but his own curiosity. Within the year he resigns his post as mining inspector and begins, in earnest, to plan the journey no one yet knows will be to the Americas.
suggested_refs: Humboldt family papers, Staatsbibliothek Berlin

stops.name: Jena, four thousand experiments in galvanism
stops.campa: Freed and restless, Humboldt lodges at Jena and throws himself at the new mystery of the age: galvanism, the electricity of living tissue. Over months he runs some four thousand experiments on frogs, on muscle and nerve, on his own arms and back, applying zinc and silver to broken skin until he blisters and bleeds, chasing Volta's and Galvani's quarrel toward an answer neither man had reached. He publishes the results as Versuche über die gereizte Muskel- und Nervenfaser: proof, to himself at least, that the living body is a theatre of chemistry and force, not a machine apart from nature.
suggested_refs: Versuche über die gereizte Muskel- und Nervenfaser (Berlin, 1797)
Volta-Galvani controversy apparatus

stops.name: Weimar, Goethe's blessing, the taste for science reawakened
stops.campa: From Jena Humboldt walks the short road to Weimar and renews an old acquaintance with Goethe, minister and poet, who is drawn at once to the young man's electric energy and his galvanic apparatus. They perform experiments together at Goethe's house; Goethe will write that this remarkable young man deserves credit for having again aroused his own taste for natural science, dormant since his Italian years. Schiller too receives him. The circle that will one day place Schelling in Jena's chair is already forming around Humboldt's frogs and batteries: the last German constellation he sees before he leaves for the Americas.
stops.quote: The young Baron von Humboldt... deserves great credit for having again aroused my taste for natural science, which had lain dormant.
suggested_refs: Goethe's house, Weimar, site of the galvanic experiments
goethe_full.journey.json, Jena and Weimar stops (shared pin)

stops.name: Madrid, the passport of a king
stops.campa: Two expeditions fail him first, Egypt closed by Napoleon's campaign, a Mediterranean crossing blocked by war, before Humboldt and the Prussian minister at Madrid, Baron von Forell, manage what no foreigner has managed in generations: an audience with the court of Carlos IV and a royal passport opening every Spanish American possession to a private traveler's instruments and curiosity. The French botanist Aimé Bonpland, met by chance in Paris, is already his companion. Humboldt calls the permission unheard-of liberality; within weeks the two men are on the road to Galicia and the sea.
suggested_refs: Royal passport of Carlos IV to Humboldt, 1799
Aimé Bonpland portrait

segments.name: The Crossing and Cumaná: The New World Opens (1799–1800)

stops.name: La Coruña, the Pizarro sails
stops.campa: On the fifth of June, at the Galician port of A Coruña, Humboldt and Bonpland carry aboard the corvette Pizarro a small observatory of instruments: sextants, barometers, a dipping needle, a cyanometer of Humboldt's own invention to measure the blue of the sky. War and an English blockade delay the sailing three weeks more. When the ship finally clears the harbor it is bound, nominally, for Havana; fever aboard and a young Asturian dead of it will change that plan before the month is out, and send them instead toward a coast neither man has any commission to visit.
suggested_refs: The corvette Pizarro
Humboldt's cyanometer, dipping needle and sextant

stops.name: Tenerife, the summit of the Teide
stops.campa: A stop meant only for water becomes six days of wonder. Humboldt and Bonpland climb through vineyards and pine forest and pumice to the crater of the Teide on 21 June, sleep near the rim, and descend at dawn with the volcano rising clear above a sea of cloud, the first sunbeams touching its summit before they touch the men below. Humboldt will call the view from Tenerife's western coast the loveliest he has known in either hemisphere. Geobotany, the mapping of plant life by altitude and climate, the discipline that will govern his whole science, is born on this single mountainside.
stops.quote: I have never beheld a prospect more varied, more attractive, more harmonious in the distribution of the masses of verdure and of rocks, than the western coast of Teneriffe.
stops.quote_source: Personal Narrative of Travels to the Equinoctial Regions of the New Continent, vol. 1 (1814)
suggested_refs: Pico del Teide crater and summit
Humboldt's geobotanical profile of Tenerife's vegetation zones

stops.name: CUMANÁ, landfall on the Spanish Main
stops.campa: Forty-one days from Tenerife, sickness aboard turns the Pizarro from its course, and on 16 July Humboldt and Bonpland step ashore not at Havana but at Cumaná, on the pearl coast of Nueva Andalucía, the oldest Spanish town on the continent and a place that already holds, four years old and playing in its streets, a boy named Antonio José de Sucre, who will die a Marshal of Ayacucho. Humboldt is dazzled by the light, the coconut palms, the ease of a colonial world he has read of only in books; he calls it the true beginning of the New World for him.
stops.quote: The splendour of the day, the vivid colouring of the vegetable world, the forms of the plants, the varied plumage of the birds, everything was stamped with the grand character of nature in the equinoctial regions.
stops.quote_source: Personal Narrative of Travels to the Equinoctial Regions of the New Continent, vol. 1 (1814)
suggested_refs: The Castillo de San Antonio de la Eminencia overlooking Cumaná
sucre.journey.json, Cumaná birthplace (shared pin)

stops.name: Caracas, arrival at the shadow of the Silla
stops.campa: After four months among the missions and llanos east of Cumaná, Humboldt and Bonpland ride into Caracas on 21 November, guests of the Aristeguieta and Ustáriz families, in a city that still counts its notable sons in single figures. A sixteen-year-old orphan named Simón Bolívar has sailed for Spain only months before. Humboldt lodges in the cool of the valley beneath the great mountain wall the Caraqueños call la Silla, the saddle, and asks its height. No one can tell him: no one has climbed it. He resolves, within days of arriving, to be the first.
suggested_refs: Colonial Caracas, view from the valley toward the Ávila/Silla massif

stops.name: Silla de Caracas, the first ascent
stops.campa: No creole gentleman or curious amateur will risk the climb, so Humboldt hires sixteen enslaved men from the Blandín estate to cut a path up the ravines between Chacaíto and Quintero. On 2 January, barometer in hand, he and Bonpland reach the Pico Oriental of the Silla and become the first men of record to stand on it. His mercury barometer gives 2,660 meters, twenty meters from the height accepted today. From the summit the whole Caribbean coast and the green trough of the valley lie mapped beneath him for the first time in human knowledge.
suggested_refs: Pico Oriental, Parque Nacional El Ávila (Waraira Repano)
Humboldt's barometric readings of the Silla de Caracas

stops.name: Calabozo, the eels and the horses
stops.campa: On the llanos at Calabozo, unwilling to wait for the eels to tire in their pools, Humboldt persuades local horsemen to drive thirty wild horses and mules into a muddy lagoon thick with electric eels. The beasts scream and rear as the eels discharge against their flanks; two horses drown; the water itself seems to seethe. Then, before the exhausted eels can recover, Humboldt and Bonpland handle them directly, deliberately, repeatedly, dangerously, to measure the shock in their own bodies. He calls the eel a living electrical apparatus, and out of the pain in his own wrists comes the first true science of animal electricity.
stops.quote: Nothing at Calabozo excited in us so great an interest as the gymnoti, which are animated electrical apparatuses.
stops.quote_source: Personal Narrative of Travels to the Equinoctial Regions of the New Continent, vol. 2 (1819)
suggested_refs: Calabozo lagoon, site of the horse-and-eel experiment
Humboldt's diagrams of electric eel anatomy

stops.name: La Esmeralda, the Casiquiare, and the two rivers made one
stops.campa: Up the flooding Orinoco and into the Atabapo and Casiquiare, past the rapids of Atures and Maipures where the drowned Atures nation's bones still lie in cliffside caves, Humboldt and Bonpland push toward a rumor European cartography has never trusted: that the Casiquiare joins the Orinoco to the Amazon, one basin flowing into the other where geographers had drawn phantom mountains to keep them apart. On 10 May, below the mission of La Esmeralda, they enter the channel and, ten days upon it, prove the bifurcation with their own instruments, the last great blank space of northern South America's rivers filled in for good.
suggested_refs: Map of the Casiquiare canal, Orinoco-Amazon connection
The rapids of Atures and Maipures

segments.name: Cuba, New Granada, and the Equator: Quito and Chimborazo (1800–1802)

stops.name: Havana, the first Cuban winter
stops.campa: Twenty-five stormy days from the Venezuelan coast bring Humboldt and Bonpland to Havana in December, where they will stay three months, guests of the reformist planter Francisco de Arango y Parreño. Humboldt studies the island's sugar economy, its slave trade and its geology with the same appetite he gave the Orinoco, gathering the statistics that will become his Political Essay on the Island of Cuba, the first work to lay Cuban demography and commerce before Europe in hard numbers and, in time, a weapon in the hands of Cuban abolitionists.
suggested_refs: Humboldt's Ensayo político sobre la isla de Cuba (1826)
Colonial Havana, 1800

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the walls of New Granada
stops.campa: A change of plan, word reaching him that the French expedition to the Pacific he had hoped to join under Baudin has already sailed without him, sends Humboldt not toward Mexico but up into New Granada instead. He lands at Cartagena in March, behind the same stone walls that a fugitive Bolívar will write his first manifesto beneath twelve years later, and begins the brutal climb of the Magdalena River toward the cordillera, long before either man could have guessed how their two Americas would meet.
suggested_refs: Walls of Cartagena de Indias (UNESCO)
bolivar.journey.json, 'Cartagena de Indias, the Manifesto' (shared pin)

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the herbarium of Mutis
stops.campa: After the Magdalena and the mule paths of the Quindío, Humboldt reaches Bogotá on 6 July and is received by José Celestino Mutis, director of the Royal Botanical Expedition to New Granada, who opens to him twenty years of unpublished botanical drawings, thousands of plates the Spanish crown has never let leave the colony. Humboldt is astonished at the older man's patient, solitary achievement and will dedicate his own first botanical volume to him. Two months among Mutis's specimens sharpen the eye Humboldt will carry, within the year, up the flank of a mountain no one has yet dared to measure from within.
stops.quote: as a simple mark of our admiration and our gratitude
stops.quote_source: Dedication of Plantes équinoxiales to José Celestino Mutis (1808)
suggested_refs: José Celestino Mutis's herbarium and the Flora de Bogotá plates
Royal Botanical Expedition to New Granada archive

stops.name: Quito, the volcanoes and young Montúfar
stops.campa: Over the páramo of Pasto and the deep trench of the equator's Avenue of Volcanoes, Humboldt reaches Quito in January, worn thin by cold and altitude sickness. Here he takes on a fourth companion who will outlast the expedition itself in the memory of a continent: Carlos Montúfar, a young quiteño creole of twenty-one, who attaches himself to Humboldt's instruments and follows him through Peru, Mexico, Cuba and the United States before returning home to die, in 1816, before a royalist firing squad as one of the first martyrs of Ecuadorian independence.
suggested_refs: Colonial Quito and the Avenue of Volcanoes
Carlos Montúfar portrait tradition

stops.name: CHIMBORAZO, the summit that was not the summit
stops.campa: On 23 June, with Bonpland, Montúfar and a handful of local men, Humboldt climbs the snow slopes of Chimborazo past the point where the porters, terrified, turn back. A crevasse and a wall of unstable ice halt them at roughly 5,878 meters, short of the summit but higher than any human has stood and lived to report it, a record holding for twenty-nine years. Fingers bleeding in the thin dry air, blood starting from his eyes and gums, Humboldt takes his readings anyway: temperature, pressure, the blue of the sky, the last mosses on the rock. Of the whole ascent he will say that nothing in nature stands isolated: one common chain links all organic being.
stops.quote: Nothing appears isolated; the chemical principles that were believed to be peculiar to animals are found in plants; a common chain links together all organic nature.
stops.quote_source: Personal Narrative of Travels to the Equinoctial Regions of the New Continent (1814–1829)
suggested_refs: Naturgemälde, Humboldt's cross-section chart of Chimborazo's vegetation zones (1807)
Chimborazo summit and the 1802 high-altitude record

stops.name: Callao, the transit of Mercury, the cold current
stops.campa: Down from the sierra to the Peruvian coast, Humboldt sets up his instruments at the port of Callao and on 9 November observes the planet Mercury cross the face of the sun, a clean astronomical fix for the whole west coast of South America. Wading and sounding the offshore water, he measures a current running cold and north against every expectation of a tropical sea, thick with the guano-covered islands whose fertilizing power he is the first European to describe in scientific terms. Cartographers will name the current for him within his own lifetime, over his mild protest that Peruvian fishermen had always known it.
suggested_refs: Callao harbor and the offshore guano islands
The Humboldt (Peru) Current

segments.name: Mexico and the Republic of Jefferson (1803–1804)

stops.name: Acapulco, landfall on the Pacific of New Spain
stops.campa: A last-minute change of plan, word that plague closes the port of Guayaquil to safe embarkation, sends Humboldt north instead of home, and on 23 March he lands with Bonpland and Montúfar at Acapulco, the great Manila-galleon port of New Spain. What was meant as a brief stop before a ship to the Philippines becomes, instead, nearly a full year inside the wealthiest and most populous of Spain's American kingdoms, an accident of shipping that will give the world Humboldt's Essai politique sur le royaume de la Nouvelle-Espagne, the first modern statistical portrait of Mexico.
suggested_refs: Colonial Acapulco and the Manila galleon trade
Ensayo político sobre el reino de la Nueva España (1811)

stops.name: Guanajuato, into the Valenciana mine
stops.campa: In the silver city of Guanajuato, Humboldt the trained mining engineer descends nearly two hundred meters into the Valenciana, the richest single mine on earth, among three thousand workers cutting silver ore by candlelight far below the cathedral bells. He measures, weighs and calculates the colony's whole mineral output with a bureaucrat's thoroughness and a geologist's wonder, and concludes, against every Spanish assumption, that Mexico's wealth lies less in its mines than in its soil and its people, could the colony ever govern itself to use them.
suggested_refs: Valenciana silver mine, Guanajuato
Humboldt's statistical tables on New Spain's silver production

stops.name: Veracruz, the last American port
stops.campa: Three hundred and fifty days in Mexico end at Veracruz on 7 March, where Humboldt, Bonpland and Montúfar board ship for a last brief call at Havana to recover papers and specimens left in trust there in 1800, before the Atlantic crossing home. Behind them lies a continent measured almost end to end: volcanoes climbed, rivers charted, mines descended, five years and ten thousand plant specimens gathered; and ahead, for a few weeks yet, one more New World port before Europe.
suggested_refs: Colonial Veracruz harbor and fortress of San Juan de Ulúa
bolivar.journey.json, 'Veracruz and Mexico City' (shared pin)

stops.name: Philadelphia, the delegation of Charles Willson Peale
stops.campa: Landing at Philadelphia in May, the first stop of a brief, unplanned detour through the young United States before the ship home to France, Humboldt is welcomed by the painter and naturalist Charles Willson Peale, tours his museum of curiosities, and writes at once to the President asking the honor of paying his respects to a philosopher admired, he says, on two continents. The American Philosophical Society opens its rooms to him; the newspapers, which months before had reported him dead in the wilderness, now cannot print enough about the returned traveler.
stops.quote: I hope I can have the good fortune of paying my respects to you in person and admiring at close range a philosopher-magistrate who is admired on two continents.
suggested_refs: Charles Willson Peale's Philadelphia Museum
American Philosophical Society, Philadelphia

stops.name: Washington, the President's House, and Jefferson
stops.campa: Peale leads the party down to Washington, and on 1 June Humboldt is received at the President's House by Thomas Jefferson himself, who wants above all his fresh intelligence on the borders of Louisiana and the Spanish provinces beyond it. Over several days of dinners and long talk the naturalist and the philosopher-statesman find each other's equal: Jefferson presses him for maps of Mexico's silver country; Humboldt, delighted, supplies them, and declines, for want of time before his ship sails, the standing invitation to see Monticello. The correspondence the visit opens will run, unbroken, until Jefferson's death.
suggested_refs: The President's House (White House), 1804
Jefferson-Humboldt correspondence, Founders Online

segments.name: Paris, the Great Decades, and a Question from Caracas (1804–1827)

stops.name: Bordeaux, Europe again, and a man risen from the dead
stops.campa: On 3 August the frigate drops anchor at Bordeaux and Humboldt, whom several European newspapers have already buried in the American wilderness, walks ashore very much alive, thirty-four years old, with sixty crates of specimens still following by sea. Save for Bonaparte himself, within weeks he is the most talked-of man on the continent: the philosopher who climbed higher than any man alive, who tamed electric eels, who dined with the President of the United States. Paris, not Berlin, is where he means to write it all up, and Paris is where he now turns.
suggested_refs: Bordeaux harbor, 1804
Contemporary press notices of Humboldt's 'resurrection'

stops.name: Paris, a question from a young Venezuelan
stops.campa: In the salons of Paris, fresh from the Americas and already a legend, Humboldt is sought out by a rich, restless Venezuelan of twenty-one named Simón Bolívar, who asks him plainly whether his country is ripe for independence. Humboldt answers, by every account, exactly as he sees it: ripe, yes, but he can name no man capable of achieving it. Bolívar carries the sentence like a wound for the rest of his life, and will climb a Roman hill within the year to answer it with an oath Humboldt never asked him to swear.
stops.quote: I believe your country is ripe for independence — but I see no man capable of achieving it.
stops.quote_source: Tradition of the Paris meeting of 1804/1805, recorded in Bolivarian biographical literature (Masur; O'Leary tradition)
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json, 'Paris, Humboldt's answer and the return of the teacher' (shared pin)
Salon of Fanny du Villars, Paris

stops.name: Naples, Vesuvius in eruption
stops.campa: Touring Italy in 1805 with the geologists Leopold von Buch and Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, Humboldt reaches Naples in time to watch Vesuvius itself erupt. The three men climb the smoking cone repeatedly through the summer to take readings no one has taken from inside an active eruption before. Venezuelan tradition places the young Bolívar at his side on this same slope, measuring the volcano's fire against the fire he has just sworn, on Monte Sacro, to carry home; whether or not he stood there, the image the two Americas keep is of the age's greatest naturalist and its future Liberator, side by side, staring into the same mountain.
suggested_refs: Vesuvius eruption of August 1805
bolivar.journey.json, 'Naples, the ascent of Vesuvius' (shared pin, traditional)

stops.name: Paris, the Circular from Missouri
stops.campa: A broadside reaches the naturalist's Paris desk from a captain of the Missouri frontier named John Cleves Symmes, a printed Circular declaring the earth hollow, open at the poles, habitable within concentric spheres, and naming Baron Alexander von Humboldt, with Humphry Davy and Samuel Mitchill, among its chosen protectors. Humboldt, who has himself stood inside a live volcano and sounded the deepest mine shafts of two continents, gives the Circular no protection at all, no letter, no lecture, not a line of print. Symmes waits in vain for the endorsement of the man whose name he has borrowed; the silence is the whole of Humboldt's polite and total refusal.
suggested_refs: symmes.journey.json, 'St. Louis, the call for one hundred brave companions' (shared reference, Circular No. 1, 10 April 1818)
Symmes's Circular No. 1, naming Humboldt as protector

stops.name: Paris, the thirty volumes
stops.campa: For twenty-three years, with brief returns to Berlin, Humboldt makes Paris his workshop: engravers for the plates, French savants for collaboration, printers for the thirty enormous volumes, the Personal Narrative, the Political Essay on New Spain, the Geography of Plants, the Views of Nature, into which the American journey is slowly, ruinously, distilled at his own expense. He befriends and corresponds with half of learned Europe from this desk; a young Charles Darwin, still at Cambridge, reads the Personal Narrative and says nothing else has ever stirred his zeal so much. The fortune of Tegel drains away, book by unfinished book.
stops.quote: Nothing ever stimulated my zeal so much as reading Humboldt's Personal Narrative.
stops.quote_source: Charles Darwin, recalling his reading of Humboldt (Autobiography, 1876; Darwin Correspondence Project)
suggested_refs: Humboldt's Voyage aux régions équinoxiales du nouveau continent, 30 vols. (1805–1834)
Charles Darwin's annotated copy of the Personal Narrative

segments.name: Berlin, Russia, and the Kosmos: The Last Light (1827–1859)

stops.name: Berlin, the return, and the professor without a chair
stops.campa: His fortune spent, Humboldt accepts the pension and the post of chamberlain the Prussian king has long held open for him and, in 1827, resettles in Berlin for good. On 3 November he opens a course of sixty-one public lectures on physical geography, the Kosmos lectures, before the university's students and professors, distilling forty years of instruments and altitudes and river-crossings into a single lecture-hall in the city he left as a restless young mining inspector.
suggested_refs: University of Berlin lecture halls, 1827
Humboldt's lecture notes for the Kosmos-Vorlesungen

stops.name: Berlin, the Sing-Akademie, a thousand strangers
stops.campa: So great is the demand that Humboldt opens a second, public series in the concert hall of the Sing-Akademie, free to all comers regardless of rank or sex, unheard-of in a Prussian university city, and some thousand Berliners and foreign visitors pack the hall through sixteen consecutive winter evenings to hear him. He tells them that the highest aim of all natural science is to recognize unity in diversity: to hold every single fact of astronomy, geology, botany and climate in one mind at once, without losing the whole for the parts. It is the seed, spoken aloud twenty years before it is printed, of the book that will be called simply Kosmos.
stops.quote: The most important aim of all physical science is this: to recognize unity in diversity, to comprehend all the single aspects as revealed by the discoveries of the last epochs... and to grasp Nature's essence under the cover of outer appearances.
suggested_refs: The Berlin Sing-Akademie concert hall
Kosmos: Entwurf einer physischen Weltbeschreibung, 5 vols. (1845–1862)

stops.name: St. Petersburg, the Tsar's commission
stops.campa: Approached by Count Cancrin, the Russian finance minister, over the question of whether the empire's platinum could support a new coinage, the fifty-nine-year-old Humboldt seizes the excuse he has wanted for years: a journey into Inner Asia. He gathers the mineralogist Gustav Rose and the naturalist Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg at St. Petersburg in April, and though the imperial itinerary keeps him under close escort throughout, he sets off eastward with the same hunger for instruments and altitudes that carried him up Chimborazo twenty-seven years before.
suggested_refs: Count Georg von Cancrin, Russian Minister of Finance
St. Petersburg, 1829

stops.name: The Urals and the Siberian steppe, nineteen thousand kilometers
stops.campa: Through the summer and autumn of 1829 the party crosses the Urals to the mines of Yekaterinburg, topaz, beryl, amethyst, and the platinum that started the whole journey, then presses on across the steppe to the Chinese frontier and the shore of the Caspian Sea, nineteen thousand kilometers in all before Humboldt turns back toward Germany in December. It is his last great field expedition, thirty years almost to the season after the Pizarro cleared La Coruña, and he takes its measurements, magnetic, thermal, geological, with the discipline of a man half his age.
suggested_refs: Ural gemstone and platinum mines, Yekaterinburg
Map of the 1829 Humboldt-Rose-Ehrenberg Russian expedition

stops.name: Berlin, Schelling returns to the rostrum
stops.campa: The Prussian king summons the aged Schelling to Berlin, to the very chair where Hegel once taught, expressly to root out the pantheism his old friend's system has let loose on the age; on 15 November Humboldt sits among the overflowing crowd, Kierkegaard, Engels, Bakunin, Burckhardt among them, to hear the philosopher who once, at Jena in 1797, praised the young mining inspector's frog-and-battery experiments as poetry as much as science. Humboldt has never fully trusted Schelling's Naturphilosophie, preferring instrument to intuition, but the two old men of the German dawn share, this winter evening, one more room.
suggested_refs: schelling.journey.json, 'Berlin, summoned to slay the dragon of Hegelianism' (shared pin)
University of Berlin aula, 1841

stops.name: Berlin, Kosmos, volume the first
stops.campa: Twenty years after the Berlin lectures, Humboldt publishes at last the first volume of Kosmos: his attempt to hold the whole of physical creation, from the nebulae to the mosses of Chimborazo, inside one continuous chain of causes and effects. It sells out in two months; within six years eighty thousand copies will have gone out from Germany alone, translated into every literary language of Europe. He is seventy-five, still climbing no mountain higher than his own writing desk, and still insisting, as he insisted on the Teide, on the Orinoco, on Chimborazo, that nothing in nature stands alone.
suggested_refs: Kosmos, vol. 1 (Stuttgart/Tübingen, 1845)
Humboldt's writing desk, Oranienburger Straße, Berlin

stops.name: Berlin, the last light
stops.campa: Ninety years old, four volumes of Kosmos behind him and a fifth unfinished on the desk, Humboldt dies quietly in his rooms on the sixth of May. His last recorded words look, characteristically, outward and upward rather than at himself: how glorious these sunbeams, he says, as if the earth itself were being called up into the sky. All Berlin turns out for the funeral procession; he is carried to Tegel, to the family ground he left as a young man of twenty-nine to see the world, and laid beside the mother whose death, sixty-three years before, had set him free to go.
stops.quote: How glorious these sunbeams are! They seem to call Earth to the Heavens!
stops.quote_source: Reported last words, Berlin, 6 May 1859 (contemporary obituary tradition)
